projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jesse Robert Seeley was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oral History of WWII U.S. Army Veteran JESSE ROBERT SEELEY as interviewed by on December 27, 2002 at Erlanger HealthLink Plus Office 975 East Third Street Chattanooga, Tennessee Michelle Lind, RPR Official Court Reporter WILLIE: Today is Friday, December 27th, 2002 and this is the beginning of an interview with Jesse Robert Seeley at the Erlanger HealthLink Plus Office, 975 East Third Street, Chattanooga, Tennessee. Mr. Seeley was born on March 5th, 1919 and is now 83 years old. My name is Michael Willie and I will conduct the interview. Mr. Seeley, could you state for the recording your name and its spelling, please?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Jesse Robert Seeley, S-E-E-L-E-Y.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And during which war or wars did you serve?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I've served in World War II. I went to combat in World War II and I served stateside during the Korean War and the Vietnam War.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And which branch of service?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: U.S. Air Force.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And what was your rank?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I was a flight officer during World War II.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Where were you born, Mr. Seeley?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I was born in Chester County, Tennessee. That is in west Tennessee.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Whereabouts? Around Jackson?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, close to Henderson, Tennessee.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Henderson?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes. That's about 18 miles from Jackson.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And tell me about your family. Did you have any brothers or sisters?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I had, um, only one brother and he was killed in the South Pacific during World War II.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. What was his age relative to yours?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: He was twe- -- he was four years younger than me.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Four years younger than you?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: He was killed when he was 21 years old.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. What did your dad do for a living?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: He was a carpenter.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: He was a carpenter?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And, so, you grew -- did you stay, grow up in Chester [sic], Tennessee all the way through until you went into the service?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, no, we moved to Madison County, Tennessee.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Where's that?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Jackson -- to Jackson, Tennessee.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: We moved there, I think, about 1939.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Why did you move to Jackson?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I think it was for work purposes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. All right. So you moved to Jackson -- or to -- you moved to Jackson, basically, and then, um, were you living there when you -- when you joined the service?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes, I was living in Jackson when they -- when they mobilized the 117th Infantry and, of course, that put me on active duty.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you were in the National Guard?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How long had you been in the National Guard?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I had only been in it a couple of months when it was mobilized.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So you joined the National Guard and then you're there a couple of months and then they mobilize?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And around what year is this?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: 1940. It's September 16th, 1940.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. September 16th, 1940, and how old are you at this time?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And were you single, married, in a relationship?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I was single at that time, yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you were single. Were you seeing anybody seriously that you --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, uh-uh.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, anyway, you go. When they mobilize, where do they send you?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: To Fort Jackson, South Carolina.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Fort Jackson, South Carolina. All right. And how long after you find out that they're getting the group together, how long do you have before you have to leave?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, it was pretty quick. I don't know. Maybe a week or something.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I don't know. I don't remember --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So, you didn't have, like, 30 days or two weeks?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No. I don't think so, no.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, they send you to Fort Jackson, South Carolina.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What's that like?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, that -- of course, this was in the infantry and -- and tell you, a lot of marching and, you know, hiking and -- with packs and everything like that. And, um, of course at -- in September it was hot in South Carolina, so --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I bet. All right. And had you already done any kind of training as a member of the National Guard?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, very little. I had very little.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you're in Fort Jackson, South Carolina and you're there training, basically, and how long are you there in Fort Jackson?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I was there for 11 months and then I took a short discharge and reenlisted in the regular Army Air Force.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: So I went from the Infantry to the Army Air Force.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Why did you do that?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I just thought I'd like it better.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Had you ever flown before?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, I hadn't at that time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, maybe except in a small plane.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. But -- okay. So, you take your discharge and then you join the Air Force immediately, and around when was this?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: That was in August of 1941.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And when you joined the Air Force -- or was it the Air Corps at that time?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: It was the Army Air Force.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Army Air Force.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Then where do you go?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I went first to Fort McPherson, Georgia. Then they sent me to Jefferson Barracks, Missouri, and then from there I went to Puerto Rico.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: To Puerto Rico?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, at Fort McPherson or Jefferson, were you -- were you learning to fly there? Is that what you were doing?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, I wasn't. While I was in, um, Puerto Rico I applied for aviation cadet training and, um, I was asked to be a -- talked to -- was interviewed by a board, and the colonel on the board told me that I would -- I told him I wanted to be a fighter pilot, and he said I would be a fighter pilot. I came back to the states to a classification center in Nashville and they classified me as a navigator, and I told him, well, I was promised I was going to be a fighter pilot. And they said, well, said, everybody wants to be a pilot and nobody wants to be a navigator. Said, you're going to be a navigator, so I was a navigator.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So, at that time was the navigator also the bombardier? Is that --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, we had a navigator and a bombardier.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: So, then I went to -- I went to navigation training at San Marcos, Texas.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And it was while I was at San Marcos, Texas in navigation school that I married my wife, Virgie Lee Seeley.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, had you known her before or did you -- (SPEAKING SIMULTANEOUSLY - INAUDIBLE)

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes, I did. I knew her before and, um, had known her for -- probably several years, I guess, I'd known her. And she came to --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was that back in Jackson then?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes, in Jackson. And she rode a troop train to Austin, Texas and we were married in Austin, Texas.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Okay. So, was she living with you there when you were doing your navigation school?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes. Well, yes or no. Actually, um, she stayed in town during the week and I only got to go into town on the weekends, so on the weekends --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. But you got to see her on the weekend?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And what was navigation school like?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, it was lots of -- I mean, you had physical training and then you had your schoolroom work and then you had your flying training all the time. And it was extremely hot there, so you would go out and get in -- we had an AT-7. It was one of our trainers, and you'd get in it. It was made out of aluminum, and you get in it and it was -- been sitting on the concrete out there all day in the hot sun, and it was -- would be really hot. And you'd take off, usually somebody'd get sick, you know. Rough air. So it was, um --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you like it then? Did you like --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I wouldn't say I liked it, but I put up with it and made it through all right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, how long are you at navigation training?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Um, let's see. About -- I think it was only nine or -- nine weeks or something, I believe. I'm not real sure anymore.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. But your navigation training, around what time of year is this? Are we getting close to --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I graduated on August the 5th, 1943.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Now, I entered cadet training in January of '43, so --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: So, I mean, I was in cadet training, I guess, about eight months altogether.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And had your brother joined the service at this time?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, he didn't join until '44, I think it was.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So, you're in naviga- -- or you finish -- you graduate from navigation school?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes, and then I go to Shreveport, Louisiana. No, I beg your pardon. I went to Alexandria, Louisiana. Alexandria Army Air Base for what they call phase training on B-17's. That was more or less a familiarization with B-17's.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And, so, is this all you're doing then, are you just flying?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes. Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And are you in a -- are you in a crew now?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes, I --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Are you in --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes, I'm in a crew.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I had a ten-man crew.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And, so, your job is the navigator?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And what is the job of the navigator on a B-17?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, of course, the navigator is to plot the course and steer the -- you know, give the course and steer the aircraft -- aircraft to its destination to get it where it's going.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And are you learning -- did you learn how to navigate by the stars or by --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes, that was -- (SPEAKING SIMULTANEOUSLY - INAUDIBLE)

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right. We learned celestial navigation and what they call, um, dead reckoning and, of course, we used radio and, um, we -- you only used the stars in the states. I never did use it overseas. Never did use the celestial overseas.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. But you were actually being trained to be able to find your way?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So, you're -- did you say you're in Alexandria?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, where did you go from Alexandria?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: From Alexandria -- now, my wife was there with me in Alexandria and she returned to Jackson, Tennessee and I went -- went to England and that was in October of '43.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you're given orders to go --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: At this time are you with a -- are you with a team, with a group at that point that you're gonna be flying with, or are you -- (SPEAKING SIMULTANEOUSLY - INAUDIBLE)

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, no, just -- I was in what they call the Lundell Provisional Group at Alexandria, but I left that when I went overseas, and, of course, my crew went together, so....

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Now, we -- we went over by ship. We were supposed to fly, but the last minute they changed and sent us over on the Queen Mary. Sent us to Scotland. We landed in Scotland.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. What was that -- what was the boat ride like for you?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, it was crowded. I think it had 10,000 soldiers on it, so....

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And you take that to -- did you say Scotland?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And is that your final destination or --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, from there I went to a place called Devizes down in Southern England in a swampy area, and then from there I went to Chelveston, C-H-E-L-V-E-S-T-O-N, Air Force Base, Air Base, which is close to North -- Northampton and Cambridge, up in that area north of London.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And I was with the 8th Air Force there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, this is your base? There is where you fly out of?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you say Chelveston?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Chelveston.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Chelveston. Okay. All right. So -- and you're with the -- I'm sorry?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I'm in the 8th Air Force, 305th Bomb Group.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: 8th Air Force. 305th --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- Bomb Group.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now, how you feeling at this time? Are you -- are you -- are you a little nervous? Are you anxious, or do you have any feelings at all about being there?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I -- I wasn't really nervous, I don't guess, and for a while there we were taking practice missions and still training, you know, and, um, of course, I was used to flying so it didn't really bother me.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Well, were you -- you did specifically the navigation. Did you have to train on any other aspects of the -- of the aircraft?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No. Now, one thing we -- we got a new navigation aid there in England. We got what they called a G-box, and I'd never seen one or heard of one till we got to England and they told me to go -- I was going to have to go take lessons on the G-box, and I asked 'em what they were talking about. And it was a little, um -- had a little screen that you got lines and -- on it and it -- calibrations, and from that you could get a -- show where you were on a radio signal and you could actually get 'em to cross and get your exact location, or you could home on it either, so....

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So, how long did it take you to learn the G-box?

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Are we talking days or weeks or --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, only a week or two, I guess, or something.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So, you're with the 8th Air Force, 305th Bomb Group?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And, um, how long have you been -- by the time you finished this -- the G-box training, was that immediately when you got over there or --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: So, you've been away from home for maybe three weeks or so, something like that?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: (Nodding head.)

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And then what happens? Tell me about your -- do you remember your first mission out?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I was -- I went over with, um, Lieutenant Gooden's crew and, um, on November the 26th, 1943, they pulled me off of a crew to substitute on another crew.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And, um, went on a mission to Bremen, Germany.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What was your target in Bremen?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I believe it was the submarine pens, but, um, in the movie Memphis Belle, you know that's where they were supposed to be going was to Bremen.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And when we -- after we crossed the coast of Germany, we started picking up flak and, um, knocked out one of our engines. We managed to go ahead and bomb the target, but, um, after we left the target we had about 100-mile-an-hour tailwind going in, and, of course, that was a headwind coming out.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And we couldn't keep up with the formation coming out, so after we dropped out of formation and then the fighters, Me 109's, started attacking us. And the first pass they came in from the nose, and myself and the bombardier were in the nose and we, of course, fired. We both had .50-caliber machine guns and we fired. And next time they came in from the tail, and I found out later that the tail gunner had -- he bailed out, and I don't know why. He thought we was going down or something, I guess. So, from that time on, they just come in from the tail and they'd sit back there, and they had 20-millimeter cannons they were firing and --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And nobody shooting back at 'em?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No -- well, basically, I guess not. And, um, we lost two more engines and we dropped, um, 13,000 feet, from 26,000 to 13,000. Um, it was at that time we were given order to bail out. I bailed out in the -- behind the bombardier and -- no, I bailed out in front of the bombardier. I bailed out behind the engineer. We had a little escape hatch, a little hatch there that I pulled the handle on it and pulled a wire out of the hinges and dropped it off and then, um, the engineer bailed out and then I bailed out and then the bombardier was behind me. Um, of course, it took a pretty good while to float down from 13,000 feet.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I landed in a tree, in a fir tree I guess it was, and my parachute was hung up there and I had to unhook my parachute and climb down, and then when I got on the ground I got under some low-lying branches of the -- of a tree and raked leaves and pine straw up over me as I lay back so that I could be covered up.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: German soldiers walked probably within five or six feet of me and didn't find me, so I decided, well, I'd move over into some bushes across a little road, and, so, I did, and I got over there and was hiding in the bushes and the Germans had gone back and gotten a dog, and they used a dog to track me down, and next thing I knew, I was looking in the end of a rifle and --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What about the rest of your crew?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, one of -- the engineer was killed. I don't know how. He -- when he bailed out -- he bailed out in front of me. He was okay then. But when he -- later on when we were on the ground, the Germans said his parachute was never opened. That -- so he was killed. And two of our waist gunners were wounded, but they weren't wounded real bad. A shell had exploded in the waist and wounded them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you're captured?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah, I was captured, and when I got -- they took us into Oldenburg and, um, when they took us -- I guess it was a police station and took us upstairs. In this room we were in upstairs, the rest of my crew were there except the one that got killed. And also while we were there, some of the German fighter pilots came in and talked to us while we were there. Some of 'em that had shot us down that day, I guess.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Could you understand, or were they translating?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah. I mean, they could speak English.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What did they say?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I mean, they just talked to us about the -- what -- the fight we had up there that day.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And discussed the -- what went on up there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Were they light? Were they -- were they light? Were they jovial? Or were they --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, yeah, they were pleasant. I mean, they --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I guess they won.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: They shot you down.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I mean, they -- they didn't -- you know, they knew it was our job, I guess, and their job, so they didn't seem too perturbed at us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So, um, at that point are you asked any other questions? Are they trying to interrogate you?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, it was after -- after that they took us to a army post and spent the night. The next day we --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What -- what were the, um -- where were you staying at the army post now? Was this like a cell?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah, it was like a cell. Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All of you together or were you --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, we were -- we were pretty much separated there.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. Could you communicate with the other guys or --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, not while I was -- at that time. The next morning they took us to breakfast. The others were there, you know, and I could. And after that they put us on a train and sent us to Frankfurt, Germany.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How are you feeling at this time? Were you scared or --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- glad to be alive?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Glad to be alive, I guess. And when we got -- reached Frankfurt, they took us to an interrogation center and put us in solitary confinement, um, and I spent six days in solitary confinement on bread and water. They took our shoes away from us, you know, as a -- to help prevent escape. Of course, you couldn't escape being in a cell anyway.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: They --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What was the interrogation --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- ____________ like, what was it like?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, when I went into interrogation, they had a German officer that, um -- he -- I sat down in a chair and, of course, he talked to me and he -- at first he was pretty nice. I mean, he offered me cigarettes and things like that. And after he saw I wasn't going to be cooperative, well, he changed and he told me that no one had been notified that I was captured and that they didn't ever have to notify anybody, and, in other words, insinuating that I could be left forever in the cell or they could do away with me, whatever they wanted to do.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah. We --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What was he asking you? What kind of questions --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, he was asking me questions about the mission and back about the base and where we came from and things like that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was there any helpful information that actually you could give them or -- or were you just --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Wasn't actually much. He -- he asked me about the course we were flying and I told him I didn't have any idea about the course. He said, well, you do. He said, you were the navigator. And I said, well, you don't know I was the navigator. He said, yes, I do. I know you were the navigator. But I never did tell him I was the navigator.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. Had somebody else told him you were a navigator or --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I -- I don't know. I guess. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Maybe he says that to everybody.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So, um -- but -- let's see. And how long did -- did the interrogation last?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, it did -- the actual interrogation didn't last very long, probably an hour or two, but they kept us there for six days in this cell.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Had you ever -- had you received any training before this about what to do in case you're captured?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you -- you basically didn't have a guideline to go by?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, nothing except they had told us to only give our rank and serial number and, you know, --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Is that --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: -- name --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- what you did then?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Name, rank and serial number. Actually, I didn't have much that would -- to give 'em, so, I mean, it --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: -- wasn't much to --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, um, you say you're there for six days?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes. And then they sent us to a transient camp on the other side of Frankfurt. We stayed there for, probably, two or three days and then they put us in a boxcar. I guess there was 50 -- I estimate 50 or 60 POWs in the boxcar.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And, um, of course, we didn't have any beds or anything in there and they -- we stayed in that five days --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Five days?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: -- on the trip. Yeah. Now, one thing I thought was a little interesting, when we got into Frankfurt -- I skipped this, but -- but we went into the railroad station and they had a big crowd of people that gathered around, around us, and had us in this -- kind of the center of the station.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And the, um, guards were -- formed a ring around us, had -- they had submachine guns, the guards did.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Were they facing you or facing --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, and they were facing the crowd. And, um, they were keeping the crowd back from us and they -- they were calling us names like (? terra fliegers, terra fliers?) and things like that. And one woman had a big heavy-handled umbrella. She burst past the guards and started hitting our radio operator over the head with it, and she brought blood and almost knocked him out before the guards got her and pulled her back. So, the people were very displeased with us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah. Now, was this an intentional spectacle or was this just something that happened when you were --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: It was just happened. I mean, they -- they --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: They didn't actually parade you in front of the crowd?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No. No, they didn't. They just -- they just -- while we were in the station there this happened.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So, you say you're on the -- the train for, you said, five days?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes, we were in the boxcar for five days.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Were you given any food?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: We were given some food. I don't really remember what it was now, but we were given some food.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Were you able to mark time at all during this, or were you trying to mark time or were you just -- what were you doing, actually doing?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: We were just -- just laying around in the boxcar mostly. I mean, the --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. And what was the mood of the people here?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, they weren't -- it wasn't too bad. It -- um, you're -- you're in the same fix as everybody else in there and everybody else is -- they're no worse off or better off than you, so you kind of -- if they can take it, you can too, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Do you remember anybody in particular that you talked to during this time?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, of course, there was three, um -- three other members of my crew in the boxcar with me, so I could talk to them.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. And did you know them very well? You said you were --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, I didn't. I didn't know them really at all. Um, and, um, I didn't really get to know 'em very well until after we were shot down.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Now, the bombardier, we were in the nose of the aircraft together, so I, you know, had a few hours with him before we got there, so I knew him better than any of 'em, I guess.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. I'm sorry. I must have missed it. The tail gunner, was the tail gunner there?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No. Now, the tail gunner, um, he was captured and brought into the camp, but when we left Frankfurt they sent the, um, enlisted men to another camp, a different camp from us. They sent us to Stalag -- Stalag Luft I, which is up on the Baltic Sea, but they sent the enlisted men to another camp, so we didn't see them anymore.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So, you're sent to -- you're on the -- you're on the train then for, like, five days?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And then is that where you end up?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: It's at Stalag Luft I, yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Then did -- do they actually take you into the camp on the train?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, we get off the train in Barth, Germany --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: -- and marched to camp. We all had to march to the camp.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: How far was that?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: It wasn't far. Only a mile or two, I guess.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Need to stop tape. (START OF PART 2 OF RECORDING)

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you had to march to camp. And what's the name of this place?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Stalag, S-T-A-L-A-G, Luft I.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Luft --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: The Luft is for air, of course.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: It was a Air Force camp.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, you're actually there with other -- all other Air Force?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, first of all, what's your feeling when you're coming in here, when you're marching here?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, of course, it wasn't a good feeling, but I wasn't -- I wouldn't say I was overanxious or anything, I mean, because I was with these other men, you know.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Of course it wasn't a good feeling to go and be behind barbed wire, be locked up.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And they had guard towers with machine guns in 'em all up and down the fence and everything, so that was a little disconcerting too, but --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And -- and where are you generally in -- in Germany at this point?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, it's the very northern part of Germany, up right next to the Baltic Sea.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: In fact, we could see the water from where -- from the camp.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So, you're sent here. What's your -- do you -- do you start thinking, I wonder how we can get out, or if I can get out, or are you just --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, we did think about that. In fact, we had quite a few tunnels that were dug, and none of us ever got out. In fact, I had a tunnel that was under my bunk at one time there, but, um, I never did -- didn't get but a few feet with it. But some of the tunnels reached all the way to the fence, but the only person that I knew to escape was a British paratrooper, I believe he was, and he was brought back later, so, um, it wasn't an easy place to escape from.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, let's talk about the first moments when you actually come into the camp. What is your initiation to the camp? Are you -- are you gathered together and spoken to at this time or....

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: The best I remember, they just took us directly to the barracks without talking to us or anything, to the barracks that we were in. I was in what we called Block 2, Room 8 and I had 27 other men in the room with me.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And -- okay. So, you're sent straight to the barracks at this point?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What's the mood?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, one thing they did do, they -- shortly after we arrived, they took us to a shower and put some kind of disinfectant on us to kill the lice, I guess, and it was very smelly, and then we had to take a shower in the -- in the shower to wash it off.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And....

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So, then you -- you're with the rest of the people in your - in your barracks, right?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And then at this point, what is the mood? What's -- what's the talk about? Is it quiet? Are people talking?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, we pretty much talked about lot of things. We talk about home and -- you know, and things like that, and food. Of course food was one thing that was talked about, 'cause we -- the rations were pretty slim. Mostly we received barley soup and potatoes, and then we did receive some Red Cross parcels, too, but....

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. How did you get the Red Cross parcels?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: They brought 'em into, um -- stored 'em in a flak building that was close by called flak -- well, now, I'm not sure what it was called, but it was a -- where they, I guess, trained people to do flak -- fire flak guns and -- but anyway, they'd bring 'em from the other end of camp by truck.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So, what -- what was life like at the prison camp? What -- what did you do?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, we -- I mean, that was -- we didn't do anything. That was something. It was a little monotonous, you know. I mean, we -- every day was just about the same.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. I mean, did you play card -- how -- did you find any way to -- for recreation, anything to do with your time?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, not really. Um -- um, somewhere I think from the Red Cross or somewhere we got a few baseballs and things like that we used to get out and play with.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Out in the outside.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And how -- were you marking time at this point?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah, mostly just marking time.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And let me see. Do you remember any -- any -- were you -- let's see. Do you remember any people who were in here? Did you make any friends, contacts here that you would keep up with in later years?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, yes. The bunk -- we had double bunks and the bunk above me was George Sardess [ph]. He lives in New Orleans and, in fact, he just called me a couple of days ago. The bombardier that I was in the nose with when we was shot down, we had a reunion in Memphis in October and I saw him in Memphis, and also saw the pilot of the aircraft and the ball gunner in Memphis. Saw 'em all, so -- and the daughter of, um, our copilot. He was a substitute also, the copilot was, so I saw her, too.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So, you were, actually -- how long were you actually in the prison -- prisoner-of-war camp?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Little over 17 months.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Little over 17 months?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And were you able to communicate at all with, um -- with your wife at home or with your family?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: We could write letters, and it took a long time for the letters to go back and forth. I think I was there probably about six months before I received my first letter.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And, in fact, my son, um -- oldest son was born while I was there and I didn't know about it until -- I think he was born in May of '44 and I didn't know about it until July, I think it was, before I found out about it.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. All right. So --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Then, as I told you before, my brother was killed in the South Pacific and I didn't find out about that until after I got out.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Do you know where in the South Pacific?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, he was -- he went down at -- over Mindanao, which is part of the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Okay. All right. So, you're in -- around what time of year was it when you went into the prison -- into the prisoner-of-war camps, Stalag Luft?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, I went down on November the 26th, and by the time I got to Stalag Luft I, it was December, early December.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. So you -- you actually get there in December and then --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I stay there until May of '45.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And you're not -- I mean, there's nothing you can do to -- is there -- do you remember any stories about anything that people did to relieve tension, any jokers, practical jokers or --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Oh, they did practical jokes and things. I mean, they --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Do you think --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: -- would do that. Like, we had a latrine in the building. Somebody'd be on it and they'd slip up behind and flush it, you know, and stuff like that. (Laughing.)

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah, they'd do jokes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. And, so, you were just basically marking time then?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: From that point on. All right. Were you able to keep up at all with what was going on in the war?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Not much. We didn't -- mostly we would learn from the new -- as new people came in, you know, we could ask them about what was going on.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And were you -- what were the guards like? Were you actually interacting with the guards?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Not very much. Some of 'em we got to know fairly well. We had one, he was -- we called him Henry the Butcher, and the reason that we called him Henry the Butcher, he was a butcher back in New York City.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And, of course, he spoke perfect English and he -- when the war came about, well, he returned to Germany and was in the German Army.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Really? And he was guarding you?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, he was one of the guards, yes.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: I'll be darned. All right. And, so, I mean, were you treated -- aside from the food, were you treated bad? Were you -- I mean, what was the treatment?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: We weren't beaten or anything like that. Um, we -- just the confinement, you know, was bad and, of course, they would -- um, if you went outside, for instance, in a air raid they'd shoot you. We had one man in my barracks that walked out the door during an air raid. He didn't know the air raid was going on, and they shot and killed him. So, I mean, it was a situation where you're -- you were in danger still, and if you were outside, they had a warning wire before you got to the main fence, and if you touched that they started firing on you with machine guns until you, if you were able to, got away. So, it was still pretty tense.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Do you remember anybody -- I mean, you told me about the tunnels that people were digging. Did you remember anyone else trying to -- trying to get out?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, there was -- I guess about every barracks probably had a tunnel, but they weren't very successful in getting out. That's the only thing.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So, any other -- anything you can particularly think of that you want to talk about while you were in the prison camp? Anything? Prisoner-of-war camp?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, not specifically. Um -- um, in -- as I told you before, I got a letter from my wife, I think it was in July of '44, telling me my son was born, and that made me happy, you know, to know about him. And, of course, he died this past April, that son did. And my brother, I didn't know about him and, um, so I didn't know -- they deliberately didn't tell me about that before I got back.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. Now, what was your prospect of getting out? Did you -- I mean, did you ever wonder how long you were going to be there or try to guess or --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, we -- we knew about the invasion and, um, of course, we were hopeful when they invaded France, you know, it wouldn't be very long, but it, of course, continued on a pretty good while.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And when we were -- did get -- when we were liberated, the Russian Army came in and we could hear the, um, guns when they crossed the Oder River to the east of us, hear 'em shelling, and a day or two later they reached the camp there. And the night before they got there, all the guards left. We woke up the next morning and all the guards were gone. And --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Did you have any idea that that was coming, that --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- it was getting close?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, we knew the Russians were close because we could hear the shelling.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And, um, the Russians -- then they came in and liberated us, and at first the commanding -- the senior allied officer that had taken over, he told us not to leave camp and -- but the Russian officer told him we were free and that -- to tear the fence down, and they did tear some of the fencing down so we could leave. And some of us went into town into Barth, which probably wasn't a real good idea, because the war still wasn't over, you know. I mean, we were still the enemy, and going into town probably wasn't a good idea, but some of us did. And, um, I think about the Russians that were there with us about probably about ten days. While they were there, they brought in a troop, like a USO troop, and put on a show for us.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And had drove in some cattle that they probably got from the Germans and killed them so we'd have some meat to eat.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was this in Barth?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah, in -- in the camp, Stalag Luft I.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. It was actually in the camp?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah. And then the allied officers got to worrying that they were Russians. They got -- getting worried that the Russians were going to take us to Russia, so they got word to England about it and the 8th Air Force flew in probably about 300 B-17 aircraft to pick us up. And the aircraft would land there at the airfield at Barth, and they never cut their engines. They'd -- they'd roll up and stop and they'd --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Load up?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: -- open the door. About 30 people would get on. They'd take off and, um -- um, they flew us to France and -- to the Camp Lucky Strike, France which was close to Rouen, France.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, what was Camp Lucky Strike?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Oh, it was just a -- more or less an assembly place for everybody, and I think -- I don't know how many people there. It must have been a 100,000 there. Um, and they told -- we -- right after we arrived, um, we were eating lunch and they told us we didn't have time to feed our -- finish our lunch, that we were -- had to catch a ship. Um, so, we went and got ready, and -- but it was a month later before we left.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah. So....

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: That was right --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Was that from Camp Lucky Strike?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, at this time were -- are you able to communicate with your wife, to send a letter across and let her know?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, not yet we didn't. Um, I think the -- well, the government did let her know that -- let my wife and mother know that I was liberated. They sent her a telegram.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: In fact, I have a copy of it there, I think. A copy of the telegram.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And how old was your son at this time?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, when I -- he was 13 months old when I got back.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. So, you're liberated by -- now, explain one thing. You said the Russians came in and liberated you?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And you said they were concerned that they were going to take you -- the Russians were going to take you back to Russia?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Why were they concerned about that?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, they got word some way, um, that they were going to. I mean, I don't know how. I guess it was -- but, you know, these senior officers or something found out something. I guess it's intelligence or something that --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Okay. So, you go to Camp Lucky Strike and you're waiting, and what's that like? What's the wait like there?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, we were in tents and, of course, it was nice to be there to us, but, um -- and we had plenty of food. The only thing is first time they filled up my mess kit, well, I couldn't eat it very much because our stomach had shrunk while we were --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: -- while we were in prisoner of war.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Right. And what is your health like at this point, aside from being really hungry?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, it wasn't bad. I mean, I'd lost a lot of weight. I think I'd lost from 150 down to about 115, so -- and by staying at Lucky Strike for a month before we went home, of course, we were getting in better shape by the time we got home. They might have done that on purpose.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: ___________+ told me. Now, um, okay. So, you finally get to go home?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And where are you flown to first?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Or are you taken by --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, I go by ship and land in, um, Camp -- I go to Camp Patrick Henry, Virginia and then I think when I'm at Camp Patrick Henry I called my wife.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And she tells me about my brother.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: What's that like? A shock?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah, it was really a shock, yeah. And then from Camp Patrick Henry they sent us to, um, Miami Beach, Florida to a rest and recreation area and they put us up in the Lord Tarleton Hotel. And my wife --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: _________. Okay. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, actually, um, my wife had -- we were -- she had joined me before this. I met her in Atlanta and we -- we drove to Miami and she was there with me in Miami, and this was really a nice hotel. It was really plush. And, um, in fact, one of the movie stars, I can't think of her -- Betty Hutton was staying at one across the street, wasn't near as good as us, so we had it pretty --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Had it pretty nice in Miami Beach.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. And was your son there with you?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No, he stayed, um, with my mother, I think.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And that's up in Jackson?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. So, you're in Miami for how long?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I'm not sure. Um, wasn't there too long, maybe a month or so, and then -- I mean, a week or so, and then I went back to Jackson and then I went to, um, Camp Gordon, Georgia. And they gave -- well, while I was at Miami, they gave me the option of getting out of the Air Force or they said I would -- could go to pilot training as a first lieutenant and, um, so I told 'em I was going to get out because, you know, what I'd been through and my brother being killed and everything, and it was pretty rough on my family, so I opted to get out. And they sent me to Camp Gordon, Georgia and then I was put on terminal leave and then later discharged. And I got out of the Air Force and stayed out for about 20 months, or 21 months and, um, in September of '47 I decided to go back in, but they didn't need -- they didn't need navigators and they didn't need -- didn't need us at all. So, to go back in, I had to go back as an NCO. I went back in as a staff sergeant and, um, then I eventually went back up. You know, I was up to master sergeant. Went back up to master sergeant. But -- and while I was -- during this time, I was -- did some time recruiting some in Chattanooga. I was on recruiting duty down at the dome building and at the federal building in Chattanooga, and then I did a tour in Alaska and a tour in -- went back to Germany for a tour.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And on the -- both times my family went with me to Germany. Went first to Germany in about '55 and we trained -- we were in a -- an outfit called a Mutual Defense Assistance Program to help train the German Air Force, see. We put 'em out of business and now we were putting 'em back into business. So -- and we went over on a ship and we came back in June of '57. We went to Italy and left out of Italy on, um, the Constitution, which was a luxury liner, and I think it took us eight days to get back to New York.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: When you were in Germany, did you visit the prison camp, or where it was?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No. Um, it was in the Russian zone, and we couldn't go -- at that time we couldn't go in the Russian zone.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. And then, um, going for -- your son, now, is how old at this time when you come back from Germany?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Thirteen months.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Thirteen months?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Now, I'm talking about when you went --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Oh, oh, no, no. Now, when we're -- went to Germany the second time, um, he was about -- the oldest son was 11, I guess, and the other one was nine or something like that.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. All right. And then you stayed in the military, right?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: And then what about during Korea? What are you doing during Korea?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: I was on recruiting duty in --

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. You were on --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Recruiting, yeah.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: -- recruiting duty? Okay. Going through and then also during Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: You were recruiting also in your --

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: No. Now, well, I'm -- yes and no. Now, I pulled a tour of recruiting duty, then I went to Alaska.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: And I spent about two-and-a-half years in Alaska and I came back to recruiting duty in Clarksville, Tennessee and then back to Chattanooga. And the Vietnam war was still going on then -- or was going on, and that's when our two sons -- my wife and I's [sic] two sons were in Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. And how did you end up in Chattanooga?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, when I was -- after I went back in the Air Force in '47, I went to Keesler Air Force Base, Mississippi. Then I was sent to San Antonio as an instructor in basic training, and while there I applied for recruiting duty and, um, I first went to Gallatin, Tennessee and Clarksville, Tennessee and then I was later recruiting in Chattanooga, so I got back to Tennessee on recruiting duty.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. But you stayed in Chattanooga; is that right?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Right. After I retired, I stayed in Chattanooga.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Now, um, how do you think being in the service during World War II and being held as a prisoner of war, how do you think that affected your life afterwards?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, when I got back I wasn't too concerned about it. I was just so glad to be back and happy to be back.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: All right. Now, you talked about how it affects more than just you, though?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Well, yes. Um, my wife, she had a long period of time there that, um, she didn't know what happened to me, you know. She didn't know whether I was killed or -- she was just told I was missing in action. And my mother only had two children. My parents. I say my mother. My father and mother only had two children and, um, I was a prisoner of war and he was missing in action in the Pacific at the same time. And her -- for instance, her half-sister asked my mother, said, how do you stand it? And she said, what choice do I have, you know. So, I mean, she didn't have any choice. But my wife, she, um -- um, was back in these circumstances and she had -- son was born and she went through a rough time with that. It was real, real rough for her.

sp.speaker: Michael Willie
sp.p: Okay. Is there anything you'd like to talk about we didn't cover in the interview?

sp.speaker: Jesse Robert Seeley
sp.p: Um, no, not really, I don't guess. We pretty much covered everything. (RECORDING ENDED)
